3D quantum-property pre-training · 5×5 cross validation · two data sets

Pre-training a 3D equivariant transformer on quantum mechanics, against the ADMET field

QuADMET-Former1 pre-trains a 1.3-million-parameter, six-layer TorchMD-ET equivariant transformer2 on PubChemQC quantum mechanical properties — total energy, HOMO–LUMO gap, dipole moment, 3D E3FP fingerprints, and per-atom Löwdin charges — across ten released single- and three-conformer checkpoints, then adapts it to ADMET endpoints by two-stage linear probing and fine-tuning (LP-FT). Its paper reports that quantum pre-training consistently beats training the same 3D architecture from scratch on TDC and Biogen ADME benchmarks. Run here on the same fifteen ExpansionRx and Biogen endpoints, 3D conformers, 5×5 cross-validation folds and held-out test sets as the rest of this site, that internal claim holds: pre-trained LP-FT beats from-scratch training on 14 of 15 endpoints (7 significant wins to 0 losses) by a median +0.083 R², beats its own frozen TabPFN 3 arm on 31 of 45 endpoint × metric combinations (losing on 12), and beats LightGBM + Morgan on 38 of 45 combinations (losing on three). Against the modern pre-trained field, fine-tuned QuADMET-Former reaches the top Tukey tier on 5 of 27 combinations on ExpansionRx (leading or tying on LogS, LOG_MPPB, and LOG_MBPB) and nearly splits ExpansionRx with fine-tuned CheMeleon6 (9 wins, 8 ties, 10 losses; 15–9–21 across both data sets), while trailing the two overall leaders: fine-tuned Atom-JEPA3 (2 wins, 8 no call, 35 losses) and Monroe + TabPFN 34 (10 wins, 2 no call, 33 losses).

The authors' architecture and checkpoints, on these folds

Both QuADMET-Former arms load the authors' TorchMD_ET from github.com/arunraja-hub/quadmetformer and their ten released pre-trained checkpoints: five quantum-property combinations ([Lw], [3D], [DM,HL,TE], [Lw,DM,HL,TE], and [All]) crossed with single-conformer and three-conformer pre-training. Every molecule uses the exact same ETKDGv3 + MMFF94 conformer cache as the Atom-JEPA study (11,129 molecules across both data sets, zero dropped). For the frozen arm (quadmet_tabpfn), each fold's held-out validation fifth selects the winning checkpoint per endpoint (03_run_tabpfn.py --select) before the test set is touched, and passes that checkpoint's 128-D graph embedding to TabPFN 35 through the exact call the Monroe arm makes.

The fine-tuned arm (quadmet_ft) adapts the 6-layer three-conformer multi_all checkpoint via two-stage LP-FT across all endpoints in each data set simultaneously (matching the multitask fine-tuning protocol of chemeleon and atomjepa_ft): Stage 1 freezes the six-layer shared_backbone and trains the shared SiLU trunk and per-endpoint heads under Kendall uncertainty-weighted Huber loss on standardized targets, restoring the best validation-MAE epoch; Stage 2 unfreezes all six equivariant layers (n_frozen = 0) with a differential learning rate and L2-SP regularization toward the pre-trained QM weights, restoring the best validation-MAE checkpoint before scoring the held-out test set.

Six arms across three representation families

The four comparators are imported unchanged from the nine-method foundation-model comparison and the Atom-JEPA study on the identical fold assignments: LightGBM on 2,048-bit Morgan counts8 (the classical floor), ChemProp7 fine-tuned from CheMeleon6 (the strongest 2D message-passing arm), Monroe + TabPFN 34 (the strongest frozen encoder read in context), and fine-tuned Atom-JEPA3 (a 39M-parameter 3D EquiformerV3 pre-trained by masked latent prediction on 19M conformers and fine-tuned multitask on the same 3D conformers).

The scoreboard

Tukey HSD per endpoint and metric, counted the same way across every study on this site: a method is on top if Tukey's simultaneous correction cannot separate it from the best mean at α = 0.05, and it is only best alone if no other arm shares the top group. The primary tables show MAE in the log10(x + 1) units of each endpoint, followed by R².

Across the two data sets, the leaderboard is led by the two heavyweights from the Atom-JEPA study: on ExpansionRx fine-tuned Atom-JEPA is on top of 19 of 27 endpoint × metric combinations and Monroe + TabPFN 3 of 9, while fine-tuned QuADMET-Former reaches the top Tukey tier on 5 of 27 combinations — posting the highest mean Spearman ρ on LogS (0.616, tied with Atom-JEPA FT), the best mean R² (0.656) and MAE (0.182) on LOG_MPPB (tied with Atom-JEPA FT), and tying for best Spearman ρ on LOG_MPPB (0.819) and LOG_MBPB (0.879). On Biogen ADME, Monroe is on top of 18 of 18 combinations and Atom-JEPA FT of 5.

Head-to-head across all 45 endpoint × metric calls

Paired by fold across all fifteen endpoints and three metrics (45 combinations), two-stage multitask LP-FT (quadmet_ft) substantially outperforms reading the frozen 128-D QM embedding in context with TabPFN 3 (quadmet_tabpfn), winning 31 of 45 combinations, tying 2, and losing 12 (17–0–10 on ExpansionRx and 14–2–2 on Biogen). Against the classical LightGBM + Morgan floor, fine-tuned QuADMET-Former wins 38 of 45 combinations (4 no call, 3 losses, going 17–1–0 on Biogen and 21–3–3 on ExpansionRx), while frozen QuADMET-Former + TabPFN 3 wins 29 (3 no call, 13 losses). Against fine-tuned CheMeleon, fine-tuned QuADMET-Former wins 15, ties 9, and loses 21 — nearly splitting ExpansionRx (9 wins, 8 ties, 10 losses) and winning all six calls on Biogen LOG_HPPB and LOG_RPPB. Against Monroe + TabPFN 3, fine-tuned QuADMET-Former wins 10 combinations on ExpansionRx (LogS, LOG_MPPB, LOG_MBPB, and LOG_MGMB) while losing 33 across both sets; against the 30× larger fine-tuned Atom-JEPA, it wins 2 (Spearman ρ on ExpansionRx LogS and Biogen LOG_RPPB), ties 8 (including all three metrics on LOG_MPPB and Spearman ρ on LOG_HPPB), and loses 35.

Choosing among the ten released QM checkpoints

QuADMET-Former releases ten checkpoints spanning five subsets of quantum mechanical pre-training targets — Löwdin atomic charges alone ([Lw]), 3D E3FP fingerprints alone ([3D]), the three molecular energy/dipole properties ([DM,HL,TE]), those three plus Löwdin charges ([Lw,DM,HL,TE]), and all five together ([All]) — each trained with either a single conformer or three conformers per molecule. Scoring all ten on each fold's held-out validation fifth shows two consistent patterns.

First, the spread from the best checkpoint to the worst is large — a median of 0.137 R² on ExpansionRx and 0.177 R² on Biogen — because checkpoints pre-trained on a single target ([Lw] or [3D] alone) generally lag the multi-property checkpoints ([Lw,DM,HL,TE] and [All]). The one striking exception is ExpansionRx LogD, where the single-conformer Löwdin atomic-charge checkpoint (Single [Lw]) ranks first on the validation fifth (0.551 R²), consistent with lipophilicity being governed by local atomic partial charges and polarity. Second, among the top multi-property checkpoints the runner-up is almost always within fold noise: across ExpansionRx (5 distinct winners) the median margin over the runner-up is 0.026 R² (0 of 9 exceeding one fold SD), and across Biogen (4 distinct winners) the median margin is 0.023 R² (1 of 6 exceeding one fold SD, on LOG_RLM).

Decomposing representation and fine-tuning

Just as in the Atom-JEPA study, the frozen TabPFN 3 arm splits the difference between Monroe + TabPFN 3 and fine-tuned QuADMET-Former into two steps: first swapping Monroe's embedding for QuADMET-Former's 128-D graph embedding under the exact same TabPFN 3 call, and second replacing TabPFN 3 with two-stage LP-FT.

Swapping Monroe's representation for QuADMET-Former's frozen embedding under TabPFN 3 reduces R² on 13 of 15 endpoints, by a median −0.130 R² on ExpansionRx (where frozen QuADMET-Former + TabPFN 3 already edges out Monroe on LOG_MPPB and LOG_MBPB) and −0.195 R² on Biogen. Testing the paper's internal claims — and auditing the released code

Why do the paper's internal ablations favour QuADMET-Former while the external leaderboard still favours Atom-JEPA and Monroe? Running four controlled internal ablations alongside a line-by-line audit of github.com/arunraja-hub/quadmetformer answers both halves of that question.

1. Quantum pre-training and LP-FT genuinely beat training TorchMD-ET from scratch. The paper's central hypothesis is internal: that pre-training TorchMD-ET on QM properties and adapting via two-stage LP-FT improves over training the same 3D architecture from random initialisation (scratch) or freezing it with a linear probe (lp). Our ablation confirms both claims directly: across the 15 endpoints, pre-trained LP-FT beats from-scratch training of the exact same multitask 6-layer architecture on 14 of 15 endpoints (7 significant wins to 0 losses) by a median +0.083 R², and Stage-2 fine-tuning improves over Stage-1 linear probing on all 15 of 15 endpoints by a median +0.348 R². The paper did not benchmark against 2D pre-trained MPNNs (CheMeleon), in-context foundation models (Monroe + TabPFN 3), or 30× larger 3D self-supervised encoders (Atom-JEPA); its baseline was its own 3D architecture trained from scratch.

2. Intermediate versus final layers under an MLP probe, and why full-backbone multitask LP-FT matters. All ten released checkpoints contain 6 equivariant attention layers (1,312,268 parameters), matching Section 3.3 of the paper, yet the repository's finetuning/downstream_train.py (line 289) restricts Optuna to num_layers ∈ {1, 2, 3}. Comparing a frozen 6-layer single-task MLP probe against a truncated 3-layer MLP probe shows why: under a frozen single-task MLP head, intermediate layer 3 edges out the final QM-specialised layer 6 on 12 of 15 endpoints (median Δ 6L−3L of −0.039 R²). Moreover, single-task unstandardized L1 fine-tuning or freezing the lower layers suffers severe test-set miscalibration on sparse/shifted endpoints (the same gap seen between single-task chemprop_st and multitask chemprop), whereas unfreezing all 6 layers (n_frozen = 0) in multitask LP-FT lifts every endpoint well above both the 3-layer and 6-layer linear probes.

Six concrete discrepancies in the released repository

Inspecting arunraja-hub/quadmetformer uncovered six bugs and paper-versus-code mismatches that affect anyone reproducing the paper from its repository; our benchmark fixes all six so QuADMET-Former is evaluated at full strength:

  1. Missing module on import (models/torchmdnet.py:10). from models.conformerAttention import * imports a file that does not exist in the repository, raising ModuleNotFoundError until shimmed.
  2. Unused periodic-table atom features (models/torchmdnet.py:374). Section 3.2 describes an 8-dimensional periodic-table atom descriptor vector data.x, and prepare_dataset.py computes and stores it, but TorchMD_ET.encode only reads data.atomic_numbers (via nn.Embedding(100, 128)) and 3D coordinates data.pos; data.x is never referenced anywhere in the model.
  3. Layer truncation and untrained out_norm (downstream_train.py:289, trainer.py:464–470). All ten checkpoints were pre-trained with 6 attention layers, and during pre-training self.out_norm (LayerNorm(128)) is never called on the molecular path (so its weights remain 1 and 0 in every checkpoint). Downstream, downstream_train.py searches only 1–3 layers, and in lpft mode trainer.py omits out_norm from the optimizer parameter groups.
  4. Untrained random layers in multi-conformer downstream mode (models/torchmdnet.py:217–225, 456–494). During pre-training, multi_conf checkpoints apply shared_backbone to 3 conformers and average their predictions. Setting multiple_conformer=True downstream instantiates randomly initialised attention_weights (384→128→3) and projection_layer (128→128) before atom mean-pooling — even in linear_probe mode, scrambling the pre-trained representations. When 3-conformer embeddings are simply mean-pooled, the Multi checkpoints beat Single on 4 of 6 Biogen endpoints. In addition, smiles_single_conf calls AllChem.EmbedMolecule(..., useRandomCoords=True) without MMFF94 force-field relaxation, contrary to Section 4.2.
  5. Evaluating the early-stopped epoch instead of the best checkpoint (downstream_train.py:446). trainer.test(final_model, graph_test_loader) is called without ckpt_path="best", evaluating the overfitted weights 10 epochs after validation loss peaked.
  6. Sign inversion on Biogen hPPB in Table 2 (finetuning/pearsonr_summary.html). In the authors' committed HTML summary table inside the repository, all four Biogen plasma_protein_binding_human (hPPB) test Pearson r values are negative (−0.2074, −0.2948, −0.1369, −0.2951), whereas Table 2 of the preprint prints the exact same four magnitudes as positive (0.207, 0.295, 0.137, 0.295).

What it costs

Because TorchMD-ET has 1.3 million parameters (one thirtieth the size of Atom-JEPA's 39M-parameter EquiformerV3) and static 5.0 Å radius graphs can be pre-computed once per molecule on GPU, evaluating all ten checkpoints across all 11,129 molecules takes under two minutes, and two-stage LP-FT in bfloat16 takes only seconds per fold across the two GPUs (apollo, RTX 5070 Ti; spark, DGX Spark GB10).

Where two methods cannot be separated, both are reported as tied.
